title: Robustify Spiking Neural Networks via Dominant Singular Deflation under Heterogeneous Training Vulnerability
claim: Training succeeds under homogeneous data regimes but collapses abruptly when a single batch comes from a different distribution.
layout: 4 panels, left-to-right, green vs red borders, checkmarks versus crosses
description: Four side-by-side panels show the same setup: image batches (a cartoon octopus, apple and snake) feed into a small two-layer network, followed by a mini plot of accuracy (red) and loss (blue) against batch. The two left panels have green borders. They show homogeneous training, first on clean data and then on adversarially perturbed data. Both end with a green checkmark and the label 'Train normally'. The two right panels have red borders and show heterogeneous training, where clean batches are followed by a perturbed batch N, marked by a dashed purple line. After that line, accuracy drops and loss jumps. Both end with a red cross and the label 'Model Collapses'. The green versus red contrast draws the eye first.
caption: The vulnerability of SNNs in heterogeneous training.
abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) process information via discrete spikes, enabling them to operate at remarkably low energy levels. However, our experimental observations reveal a striking vulnerability when SNNs are trained using the mainstream method—direct encoding combined with backpropagation through time (BPTT): even a single backward pass on data drawn from a slightly different distribution can lead to catastrophic network collapse. We refer to this phenomenon as the heterogeneous training vulnerability of SNNs. Our theoretical analysis attributes this vulnerability to the repeated inputs inherent in direct encoding and the gradient accumulation characteristic of BPTT, which together produce an exceptional large Hessian spectral radius. To address this challenge, we develop a hyperparameter-free method called Dominant Singular Deflation (DSD). By orthogonally projecting the dominant singular components of gradients, DSD effectively reduces the Hessian spectral radius, thereby preventing SNNs from settling into sharp minima. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DSD not only mitigates the vulnerability of SNNs under heterogeneous training, but also significantly enhances overall robustness compared to key baselines, providing strong support for safer SNNs.
